clue.text: A & E changing round, exit becomes entrance

indicators.note: the clue tells us the letters A and E in the exit word swap places with each other

parts.note: a getaway is an exit or escape

explanation.surface: A hospital casualty department rearranged so that the way out is now the way in.
explanation.walkthrough: A & E is the British name for a hospital casualty department, but here it just names two letters. Swapping the E and A of GETAWAY gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A gate or passage you go in through is a synonym for an entrance.

clue.text: Creatively dealing, conquer inflation

indicators.note: doing something creatively means reworking it freely, so the letters of the next two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Advice to inflate your conquests by dealing with them imaginatively.
explanation.definitionFit: Inflation of language, meaning pompous and overblown speech, is what this word for lofty style describes.

clue.text: Man's dealt with rot in timber

indicators.note: letters that have been dealt with are handled and rearranged, signalling an anagram of the words around

explanation.surface: A workman has treated the decay in some wood.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a horizontal crossbeam of wood over a door or window, so a piece of timber.

clue.text: Say financial index raised large amount

indicators.note: in a down clue something raised is read upwards, so the letters are reversed

parts.note: EG, for example, is what 'say' means when giving an instance
the Dow Jones index of US shares, the Dow for short

explanation.surface: A stock-market index going up brings in a lot of money.
explanation.walkthrough: Up a down light the order is reversed: EGDOW read upwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A British informal word for a big lump or chunk of something, so a large amount.

clue.text: Sailor may snatch rum

indicators.note: rum as an adjective means odd or strange, so the letters are put into a strange order

explanation.surface: A seafarer might grab a bottle of rum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rum' reads as the sailor's drink, but it is the adjective meaning odd, signalling the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who sails a pleasure vessel is a kind of sailor.

clue.text: Car set off with new parts

indicators.note: off here means gone bad or awry, so the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: A vehicle drove away having had replacement components fitted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'parts' sounds mechanical, but a play or film recast has new actors in its roles.
explanation.definitionFit: A production that has been given a fresh cast has new actors playing its roles, or parts.

clue.text: Nick single, not out

parts.note: in cricket a single is one run
a batsman who is not out is still in

explanation.surface: A cricketing scene: a batsman scores one and survives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nick' looks like a cricket edge in this setting, but it is the British slang verb for arrest.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are British slang for arresting someone, to nick or pull in a suspect.

clue.text: Strapless item flatters weed

parts.note: to court someone is to woo or flatter them
to hoe is to clear weeds with a hoe

explanation.surface: A boastful garment, perhaps a strapless dress, that flatters a skinny person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'weed' reads as a feeble person being flattered; it is the verb, to remove weeds.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a plain women's pump with no strap or fastening, so a strapless item of footwear.

clue.text: Left over rolls filled with end of veg served up as informal meal

indicators.note: in a down clue served up means brought upward, so the whole string is read in reverse

parts.note: O is the cricket scoring abbreviation for an over

indicators.note: the rolls are filled, so a letter is placed inside that word

parts.note: baps are soft bread rolls in Britain

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: Leftover bread rolls stuffed with vegetables make a casual supper.
explanation.walkthrough: BAPS with G inside gives BGAPS; after L and O the string LOBGAPS read upwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A casual British shortening of spaghetti bolognese, an everyday informal meal.

clue.text: Verne characters arranged to be endlessly at sea in fictional creation

indicators.note: characters that are arranged are set in a new order, signalling an anagram

parts.note: the letters of the name Verne are taken as anagram fodder
someone endlessly at sea will never reach shore, which is to never land

explanation.surface: Jules Verne's characters, endlessly afloat in an invented world.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearranging VERNE gives NEVER; the rest is a cryptic phrase for never coming ashore.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the imaginary island of Peter Pan, J. M. Barrie's invented place, a fictional creation.

clue.text: Prize fight with commercial setting

indicators.note: a commercial setting is one that surrounds the fight like a jewel's mount

parts.note: an ad is a commercial
a war is a fight

explanation.surface: A boxing bout sponsored by advertising, with a trophy at stake.
explanation.definitionFit: A trophy or honour given to a winner is a prize.

clue.text: Perhaps run through to have drink after do filled up

indicators.note: after says the drink follows the word for do

parts.note: to do someone is to con or swindle them
a jug is a jugful of drink
someone who ate has filled up on food

explanation.surface: Someone at a party has a drink and then fills up on food.
explanation.walkthrough: 'run' is the verb being inflected: run, runs, ran, running.
explanation.definitionFit: To go through all the inflected forms of a verb such as run is grammatical inflection of that verb.

clue.text: Board of examiners analysing set of statistics

parts.note: dissecting something is analysing it in close detail
a table is an ordered set of figures

explanation.surface: Exam assessors poring over a batch of data.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board of examiners' reads as a committee; it is the literal board on which anatomists examine bodies.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the bench on which anatomy students and pathologists examine bodies, a board used by examiners.

clue.text: Leeds United manager hints match officials received payment

indicators.note: the initials received, or took in, the officials, so they go inside
the hints of the three words are just their first letters, a small suggestion of each

parts.note: umps is short for umpires

explanation.surface: The Leeds United boss suggests referees took bribes.
explanation.walkthrough: The initials LUM take UMPS inside after their L.
explanation.definitionFit: A single payment of the whole sum at once, rather than instalments.

clue.text: Kept going and pressed suit, covering mark

indicators.note: the word for pressed suit covers, or goes round, the mark

parts.note: to press a suit is to bring a lawsuit, so sued
a stain is a mark

explanation.surface: Someone persevered by ironing their suit to hide a stain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pressed suit' suggests ironing; it means pursued a lawsuit.
explanation.definitionFit: Something maintained without a break has been continued, or kept going.

clue.text: Rank outsiders of Eindhoven holding Chelsea — missing main opportunity to lead

indicators.note: the outer letters hold the rest inside them
the outsiders of a word are its first and last letters
missing says a word is taken away from the club name

parts.note: the main is the open sea

indicators.note: the letter that leads a word is its first

explanation.surface: A football match report: Eindhoven's defence holds Chelsea, who miss a big scoring chance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'main' looks like 'main opportunity' in the football sense, but it is the sea taken from the club's name; PSV Eindhoven is a Dutch football club.
explanation.definitionFit: A level or grade in a hierarchy, such as the upper levels of an organisation, is a rank.

clue.text: Aim to get dodgy cleric like this?

indicators.note: the aim gets, or receives, the rearranged cleric inside it

parts.note: an end is an aim or goal

indicators.note: dodgy means suspect or unsound, signalling the letters are disordered

explanation.surface: A question of whether surrounding a shady priest is the goal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'like this' points back at the wordplay itself: the rearranged cleric is surrounded on both sides by the aim.
explanation.definitionFit: The wordplay shows a word surrounded on both sides, so 'like this' describes being enclosed.

clue.text: Making money from tobacco plug's a bad thing

parts.note: a quid is a piece of chewing tobacco
a sin is a bad thing

explanation.surface: Profiting from tobacco is wicked.
explanation.walkthrough: Quid is also British slang for a pound; being 'quids in' means being in profit.
explanation.definitionFit: This British idiom means being in profit, so it describes making money.

clue.text: Happening where Kelly was singin' in Halifax?

definitions.meaning: something under way or in progress is happening

definitions.text: where Kelly was singin' in Halifax?
definitions.meaning: Gene Kelly was Singin' in the Rain; in a Yorkshire accent like Halifax's, 'the rain' clips to t'rain

explanation.surface: A northern take on the famous film song.
explanation.walkthrough: Halifax is a Yorkshire town, where 'the' is often shortened to t'. Gene Kelly's film was Singin' in the Rain.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means in progress or under way, so happening.

clue.text: Confirm presence in audience of playwright

indicators.note: an audience hears, so the clue words are judged by their sound

parts.note: to check off a name on a register is to confirm the person is there

explanation.surface: Taking a register at a theatre performance of a dramatist's work.
explanation.definitionFit: Anton Chekhov was a Russian dramatist, author of The Seagull and The Cherry Orchard.

clue.text: House accommodating old bag

indicators.note: the house accommodates, or holds, the next word inside it

parts.note: a hall is a large country house

explanation.surface: A residence taking in an elderly woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'old bag' reads as a rude term for a woman; the words split.
explanation.definitionFit: A large soft travel bag for carrying all sorts is a kind of bag.

clue.text: Seconds in Indian restaurant unfinished? Fried cauli with side of raita, not on menu

parts.note: seconds are an extra helping

indicators.note: unfinished means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: in Britain a curry, or curry house, is an Indian restaurant

indicators.note: frying scrambles the cauli, signalling an anagram
the side of a word here is its first letter

explanation.surface: An order at an Indian restaurant: more food, cauliflower and raita.
explanation.walkthrough: Raita is an Indian yoghurt side dish. 'menu' is figurative: a school's menu of lessons, its curriculum.
explanation.definitionFit: Activities outside the school curriculum are not on its official programme, a menu of studies.

clue.text: Treatment for winged horse raised with wings clipped

indicators.note: in a down clue raised means read upwards, so reversed
clipping the wings removes the two outer letters

parts.note: Pegasus is the winged horse of Greek myth

explanation.surface: Clipping a flying horse's wings as some treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: PEGASUS loses its outer letters to give EGASU, which read upwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The way something is handled or used is its treatment.

clue.text: Goldsmith hiding identity when turning up in Spanish port

indicators.note: in a down clue turning up means read upwards, so reversed
the name hides identity inside it

parts.note: Zac Goldsmith is a British politician
ID is short for identity

explanation.surface: A politician turning up incognito in Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: ZIDAC read upwards gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Cádiz is a port city on the southwest coast of Spain.

clue.text: Old-fashioned means of protection from pyramid scam?

definitions.meaning: armour of interlinked metal rings worn by medieval soldiers
letters sent on in a chain asking each recipient to forward them, a pyramid scheme

explanation.surface: Medieval defence against a fraud of ancient Egypt.
explanation.walkthrough: The two senses are armour and the chain letter.
explanation.definitionFit: It is linked-ring armour, and also chain letters, which spread like a pyramid scheme.

clue.text: Play 9 over and over again for wife

indicators.note: the W for wife is turned over again, upside down, which makes the shape of an M
turned over means read the other way, so reversed

parts.note: 9 points to the answer at 9 across

explanation.surface: A sports report: playing a match over and over to win a prize for one's wife.
explanation.walkthrough: Reversing AWARD gives DRAWA; then W, the abbreviation for wife, turned upside down becomes M.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: any theatrical work performed on stage, such as a tragedy or comedy, is a play.

clue.text: Nervous editor's gone running outside

indicators.note: the rearranged word goes outside the editor
running suggests the letters are on the move, so rearranged

explanation.surface: An anxious editor has dashed out of the office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'running outside' reads as the editor dashing out, but 'running' is the anagram signal and 'outside' the container one.
explanation.definitionFit: Feeling edgy or tense is a synonym for nervous.

clue.text: Top Zeppelin precursors on day one caused amazement

indicators.note: on means the precursors follow the day and one

parts.note: A is the indefinite article, one
ZZ precedes Top in the band ZZ Top, and Led precedes Zeppelin in Led Zeppelin

explanation.surface: Pioneering rock bands put on a stunning show on their first day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'precursors' means the words that come before each: ZZ Top and Led Zeppelin are rock bands.
explanation.definitionFit: To dazzle someone is to amaze them, so dazzled is caused amazement.
